title: Pads, Banks & Full Level
blurb: Set the controller up for practice: confirm the pads reach PadLab, learn the two banks, and get Full Level out of your way.

steps.title: Connect and confirm
body: Plug the MPK into your computer with a USB cable and open PadLab in Chrome or Edge. Allow MIDI access when the browser asks.
The chip in the top-right of the lesson list should name your controller. Open it and hit each pad in turn.
Every pad you hit should flash the matching pad on screen. If the wrong pad lights up — or none does — run MIDI Learn in that panel and tap pads 1 to 8 in order once.
steps.checkpoint: All eight pads light the right on-screen pad, and nothing else on the controller makes a sound.
steps.tip: A learned mapping is authoritative: once you have taught PadLab your pads, the keybed, knobs, and transport buttons are ignored, so a stray knob twist can never trigger a hit mid-lesson.

steps.title: The two banks
body: The MPK has eight physical pads but two banks of assignments, A and B, giving sixteen sounds in total.
Press PAD BANK to switch. The display shows which bank you are on.
PadLab's 8-pad lessons all live on one bank — the factory Bank A notes. Leave the controller on Bank A while you practise and you never have to think about it again.
Bank B is worth knowing for the 16-pad charts: they are written for a 4x4 grid, so on an 8-pad controller you would have to bank-switch mid-bar. Use the 8-pad filter in the lesson list instead.
steps.checkpoint: You can switch to Bank B and back, and you know which bank your lessons expect.
steps.tip: If you bank-switch by accident during a lesson your hits will stop registering. That is the usual cause of a run where nothing scores.

steps.title: Turn Full Level off for practice
body: FULL LEVEL forces every pad hit to maximum velocity no matter how hard you play.
It is genuinely useful when you are programming a part and want each note identical.
It is the wrong setting for practice: the ghost-note lessons in Technique Workouts are built entirely on the gap between a soft hit and a hard one, and with Full Level on there is no gap.
Press it and check the light is off before you start a session.
steps.checkpoint: Playing a pad gently and then hard produces two clearly different volumes.
steps.tip: PadLab scores timing, not velocity — but the sound you hear back is velocity-mapped, so dynamics are how you tell whether your hands are actually doing what you think.

steps.title: Pick a velocity curve you can live with
body: The pads respond through a velocity curve that decides how hard you have to hit for a loud note. It is in the on-board settings menu on the display, or in Akai's MPK Mini editor software.
Try each curve with the same relaxed stroke and pick the one where a comfortable hit lands around three-quarters volume.
If you find yourself hammering the pads to be heard, the curve is too hard — that is a setup problem, not a technique problem, and it will wreck your timing at speed.
steps.checkpoint: A relaxed, repeatable stroke gives you a solid hit without any effort.
steps.tip: Set this before you build habits. Re-learning your stroke after changing the curve costs far more than the five minutes it takes to choose now.

steps.title: Sit down and play something
body: Rest your index and middle fingers on pads 1 and 2 — kick and snare in almost every PadLab lesson — and leave them there.
Play from the finger, not the wrist or the arm. The pad only needs a few millimetres of travel.
Open the Foundations course and run First Beats. Use Practice mode first: playback waits at each note until you hit the right pad, so you cannot fall behind.
If your hits feel systematically late even when they sound right, open the device panel and raise the input-latency slider a few milliseconds.
steps.checkpoint: You can play a bar of kick and snare without looking down at your hands.
steps.tip: The latency slider shifts judging and miss detection together, so raising it can never turn a good hit into a miss. Set it once, honestly, and forget it.
